raw_response:
It can make sense to switch, but the repeated outages in your description are a reason to evaluate a move, not enough evidence to identify a more reliable provider. I would first identify what actually stops you working: fetching code, pushing changes, reviewing contributions, running CI, or publishing releases. The best alternative depends on that boundary.

My practical recommendation is to test GitLab.com with one representative repository and maintain an independent copy of your Git data during the evaluation. For a qualifying free-software project, Codeberg is also a serious hosted option. Forgejo and SourceHut become more attractive when their operating or collaboration model suits you.

## Ranked options

1. **GitLab.com — the first general hosted alternative to evaluate.** GitLab documents importing GitHub projects, including collaboration records, but the importer does not bring over GitHub organizations or groups. Check its permissions and import limitations before trusting a migration. GitLab also publishes a separate guide for converting GitHub Actions workflows into GitLab CI/CD, so CI should be tested as its own migration task. This is a documented route to another host, not evidence that its uptime will be better for your workload. [GitHub importer](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/import/github/); [CI migration](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/migration/github_actions/). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn113172141view0","turn250146023view0","turn287527577view3"]}}

2. **Keep GitHub and add an independent Git mirror — useful if code access is the immediate problem.** GitHub documents maintaining a mirror by cloning and periodically pushing to another location; Git LFS objects have additional transfer steps. My suggested adaptation is to choose a destination independent of GitHub, establish an update schedule, and test that you can fetch from it. A mirror covers repository history. It is not, by itself, a replacement for your issue tracker, reviews, CI, releases, or an agreed write-failover process. It also cannot contain changes that have not reached it. [Mirroring guide](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/duplicating-a-repository). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn287527577view2"}}

3. **Codeberg — evaluate for free-software work.** Codeberg is a non-profit, Forgejo-based hosting service. Its suitability depends on your project: the FAQ distinguishes its free-software mission from general private commercial hosting, with limited private-content exceptions. It also describes resource and CI access requests. Since you did not specify the repository type, I would keep Codeberg on the shortlist while confirming eligibility. [Overview](https://docs.codeberg.org/getting-started/what-is-codeberg/); [FAQ](https://docs.codeberg.org/getting-started/faq/). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn113172141view2","turn287527577view0"]}}

4. **Self-hosted Forgejo — evaluate if you want to operate the host.** Forgejo supplies a self-hosted alternative, giving you a direct choice of infrastructure and operation. My inference is that this changes who carries the hosting work; it does not automatically improve availability. You would need a workable plan for updates, recovery, monitoring and any CI runners. Its v15.0 Actions documentation explicitly distinguishes familiarity with GitHub Actions from compatibility, so test your actual workflows. You have not stated whether self-hosting is acceptable, which is the main unresolved choice here. [Forgejo](https://forgejo.org/); [Actions differences](https://forgejo.org/docs/v15.0/user/actions/github-actions/). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn250146023view4","turn250146023view2"]}}

5. **SourceHut — evaluate if its collaboration model appeals to you.** SourceHut documents hosted Git repositories, CI, issue tracking, and mailing-list/patch-based review. That makes it a real alternative, but the workflow needs to work for your contributors. The current homepage calls it a public alpha. I would run a small review-and-build trial before moving an established project; this research does not establish complete GitHub metadata migration or a measured availability improvement. [SourceHut features](https://sourcehut.org/). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn287527577view1"}}

## How I would decide whether the move is worth it

Treat the migration as a small experiment. Pick a representative repository and list the things it actually depends on: contributors' access, review process, automation, deployment credentials, packages, large files and documentation. Check the imported result, run the build and release path, and have someone other than the administrator try contributing. These are suggested evaluation criteria, not requirements you already stated.

Then compare the cost of the interruptions you experience with the migration effort and the continuing cost of the new setup. If the current interruptions regularly block necessary work and a pilot succeeds, moving is reasonable. If the main need is occasional access to code while the rest of your workflow remains strongly tied to GitHub, an independent mirror may provide useful resilience with a smaller change. If CI is the bottleneck, test an independent build path rather than assuming a change of repository URL solves it.

I have not compared provider incident histories over the same period or established a reliability ranking. Nor have I assumed a budget, a preferred review process, use of GitHub Actions, or willingness to self-host. The evidence above is documentation, not an executed migration. Most pages are live and undated; they support a current shortlist, but do not prove the exact feature or policy state on the question date, 17 August 2026.
